topics.label: Sound
facts: Sound is made by vibrations, which are tiny back-and-forth movements.
Sound travels through air, water, and solid things, but it cannot travel through empty space.
Sound travels faster through water than through air.
The pitch of a sound depends on how fast something vibrates: fast vibrations make high sounds.

questions.fact: When something vibrates, it shakes the air around it and makes sound waves.

questions.q: Can sound travel through empty space?
choices: No, it needs air, water, or a solid to travel through
questions.fact: Sound needs something to vibrate through, so space is silent.
Fast vibrations make high sounds, and slow vibrations make low sounds.

questions.q: Through which does sound travel fastest?
questions.fact: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.

topics.label: Heat
facts: Heat is energy that moves from something warm to something cooler.
Heat can travel by conduction, convection, and radiation.
Metals are good conductors of heat, which is why saucepans are made of metal.
Insulators, like wool and wood, slow down the movement of heat.

choices: From cold things to warm things
From warm things to cooler things
questions.fact: Heat always flows from warmer objects to cooler ones until they are the same temperature.

questions.q: Which material is a good conductor of heat?
questions.fact: Metals let heat pass through them easily, which is why metal spoons get hot in soup.

questions.q: What do we call a material that slows heat down?
questions.fact: Insulators like wool, wood, and plastic slow the flow of heat.

questions.q: Why do we wear a woolly jumper in winter?
choices: Wool insulates and keeps body heat in
questions.fact: Wool traps air and slows heat escaping from your body, keeping you warm.

topics.label: States of Matter
facts: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, and it can be a solid, a liquid, or a gas.
In a solid, the tiny particles are packed tightly and stay in place.
In a liquid, the particles can slide past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
In a gas, the particles move freely and spread out to fill the whole container.

questions.q: What are the three states of matter?
questions.fact: Most matter is a solid, a liquid, or a gas.

questions.q: Which state of matter flows and takes the shape of its container?
questions.fact: Liquids flow and take the shape of the bottom of their container.

questions.q: What happens to water when it is heated and boils?
choices: It turns into a gas called steam
questions.fact: Boiling water turns into water vapour, a gas.

questions.q: In which state are the particles packed tightly in place?
questions.fact: In a solid, particles are held tightly together and can only vibrate in place.

topics.label: Friction
facts: Friction is the force that slows things down when two surfaces rub against each other.
Rough surfaces, like sandpaper, create more friction than smooth surfaces, like ice.
Friction can make heat: rubbing your hands together quickly warms them up.
Car tyres use friction to grip the road, which helps cars stop and turn safely.

choices: A force that slows things down when surfaces rub together
questions.fact: Friction is the force that resists motion when two surfaces rub against each other.

questions.q: Which surface creates the most friction?
questions.fact: Rough surfaces like sandpaper create more friction than smooth ones.

questions.q: What can friction make when you rub your hands together?
questions.fact: Rubbing hands together uses friction, which makes heat.

questions.q: Why do car tyres need friction?
choices: To grip the road so cars can stop and turn safely
To make the wheels spin freely
To make the car go faster on ice
questions.fact: Tyre friction grips the road, letting cars brake and steer.
